title: Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Has No Rules
excerpt: Vietnam has no registered dog meat slaughterhouses — a total enforcement vacuum that puts public health at serious risk.
body_html:
In Vietnam, an estimated 5 million dogs are killed for meat every year. Yet there is not a single registered, inspected, or regulated slaughterhouse in the entire country to handle them. That is not a minor compliance gap — it is the complete absence of a food safety framework for an industry operating at enormous scale. No veterinary oversight. No hygiene standards. No traceability. Every step of the supply chain, from theft or capture to slaughter and sale, happens entirely outside the law.

The consequences for public health are direct and measurable. Unregulated dog slaughter is a documented vector for rabies transmission — the movement of live dogs across provinces spreads the virus into areas that would otherwise be clear. Workers who handle animals in uncontrolled conditions face acute exposure risk. Consumers face contamination from E. coli and Salmonella, pathogens that regulated meat processing is specifically designed to eliminate. When there are no inspections, there are no safeguards — and when there are no safeguards, people get sick.

Other countries have demonstrated that ending the dog meat trade produces measurable public health improvements. South Korea, which has moved to phase out the industry through formal legislation, saw sustained pressure from its own public health authorities who cited disease risk as a primary driver. The Philippines banned the trade in 1998, and enforcement — however imperfect — created clear lines of accountability that unregulated markets simply cannot provide. The common thread in every successful case is that the change was framed as a public health and governance issue, not only an animal welfare question. Regulation, or the lack of it, is the core problem.

Crucially, this is not an agenda being imposed from outside. A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese people support ending the dog meat trade. That supermajority includes urban residents, younger generations, and local authorities in cities like Hanoi and Hoi An that have already issued voluntary phase-out guidance. The will for change is domestic, democratic, and decisive. What is missing is a national regulatory framework that matches the values the Vietnamese public has already clearly expressed.

Ending the dog meat trade in Vietnam is, at its foundation, a question of governance. A food industry that operates with zero registered facilities, zero veterinary checks, and zero traceability cannot be made safe — it can only be ended. The legal infrastructure, the public support, and the public health rationale all point in the same direction. Vietnam has the opportunity to close this enforcement gap permanently, protect its citizens from preventable disease, and align national policy with what 95% of its own people already want. Sign the petition and add your voice to theirs.

title: Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Has No Safety Net
excerpt: Vietnam's dog meat trade operates in a complete regulatory vacuum. Here's what that means for public health — and how other countries fixed it.
body_html:
Every year, an estimated 5 million dogs are killed for meat in Vietnam. Not one of the facilities handling this trade is registered, inspected, or held to any food safety standard. In a country with robust regulations governing pork, poultry, and seafood, this gap is not an oversight — it is a structural failure with real consequences for the Vietnamese public.

The absence of registered slaughterhouses means there is no veterinary inspection at the point of slaughter, no cold-chain verification, no testing for pathogens, and no traceability if an outbreak occurs. Dogs entering this supply chain are frequently transported in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions across provincial and national borders — a documented pathway for rabies transmission, as well as contamination by E. coli and Salmonella. Rabies, a near-universally fatal disease once symptoms appear, remains endemic in Vietnam, and the unregulated movement of dogs for slaughter directly undermines national eradication efforts.

The international evidence is instructive. South Korea, which operated a similarly unregulated dog meat industry for decades, saw measurable improvements in food safety compliance and zoonotic disease surveillance following targeted regulatory intervention that ultimately accelerated a broader legislative ban. The Philippines enacted a full ban in 1998 under its Animal Welfare Act; enforcement gaps persisted, but the legal framework empowered local authorities and health agencies to act. In both cases, reform was driven not by external pressure alone, but by domestic public health advocates and citizens who had already shifted in values.

That domestic shift is precisely what has happened in Vietnam. A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese people support ending the dog meat trade — a figure that reflects changing urban attitudes, generational shifts, and a growing awareness of the health risks involved. Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have both issued non-binding guidance encouraging the trade's end. What is missing is the legislative architecture to match public will with enforceable policy. Regulation is not the ceiling of ambition here — it is the floor. Mandatory registration of any facility handling dog meat for sale would immediately expose the scale of the problem and create accountability. Mandatory veterinary inspection would either bring the trade into compliance with standards applied to every other meat — a standard it cannot realistically meet — or accelerate its closure.

Lucky, a nine-year-old Vietnamese Tả dog, represents the millions of family companions who enter this supply chain through theft and illegal transport, with no traceability and no recourse for the families they are taken from. The regulatory vacuum does not only harm animals — it harms the Vietnamese families and communities who deserve a food system they can trust. The 95% of Vietnamese who want this trade to end are not waiting for foreign instruction. They are waiting for a legal framework that reflects their own values. title: Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Has No Food Safety Net
excerpt: Vietnam's dog meat trade operates with zero registered slaughterhouses, creating a public health crisis that 95% of Vietnamese want to end.
body_html:
In Vietnam, millions of people eat at restaurants every day with a reasonable expectation that the food on their plate has passed through some form of regulated inspection. That expectation does not apply to dog meat. Not a single dog meat slaughterhouse in Vietnam is formally registered or licensed. Every step of the supply chain — from capture to killing to consumption — operates entirely outside the country's food safety framework. This is not a gap in the system. It is the absence of one.

The consequences for public health are measurable and serious. Dogs moved through this trade are frequently transported across provincial borders without veterinary checks, creating ideal conditions for disease transmission. The World Health Organization has identified the dog meat trade as a vector for rabies spread, and studies have documented contamination with E. coli and Salmonella at processing and retail points. Unlike beef or pork supply chains — which, however imperfectly, involve licensing, inspection, and traceability — dog meat reaches the consumer with no documentation, no testing, and no accountability. When something goes wrong, there is no record of where the animal came from or who handled it.

Countries that have moved to ban or tightly regulate the dog meat trade offer a useful comparison. South Korea, which is actively legislating toward a full ban after decades of a regulated grey market, saw significant reductions in associated zoonotic disease risk as enforcement tightened. The Philippines enacted a ban in 1998 under its Animal Welfare Act, and subsequent public health data from regions where the trade was most active showed measurable declines in dog-related rabies transmission. The pattern is consistent: regulation and bans work, both for animals and for people.

What makes Vietnam's situation particularly significant is that the demand for change is not coming from outside the country. A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese people support ending the dog meat trade. That is not a fringe position or a foreign imposition — it is an overwhelming domestic consensus. Cities including Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have already issued formal recommendations to phase out the trade, citing both animal welfare and public health concerns. The regulatory infrastructure to act exists. What is needed now is the political will to apply it.

Lucky, a nine-year-old Vietnamese Tả dog and the face of the Stop Dog Eaters campaign, represents the millions of dogs whose lives depend on that political will becoming policy. But Lucky also represents something broader: the right of Vietnamese communities to live without the public health risks that an unregulated, uninspected food trade creates. Approximately 5 million dogs are killed in this trade every year. None of them pass through a single registered facility. Ending this trade is not about imposing external values — it is about enforcing the food safety and animal protection standards that Vietnam has already committed to on paper, backed by a population that is already on board.

title: Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Has No Safety Net
excerpt: Vietnam's dog meat trade operates outside every food safety framework — and the data on public health consequences is impossible to ignore.
body_html:
Every year, an estimated 5 million dogs are killed for meat in Vietnam. Not one of those animals passes through a registered slaughterhouse. Not one transaction falls under a licensed food safety inspection regime. This is not a loophole — it is a total absence of regulatory infrastructure, and it carries measurable consequences for the people who live alongside this trade every day.

Vietnam's food safety law requires all meat intended for human consumption to be processed in licensed, inspected facilities. Dog meat is consumed widely, yet exists entirely outside this framework. The supply chain — from capture to slaughter to sale — is unregulated at every stage. This means no veterinary checks, no temperature controls, no pathogen screening, and no traceability. The result is documented: the dog meat trade is a recognised vector for rabies transmission, as well as contamination by E. coli and Salmonella. These are not theoretical risks. They are recorded public health outcomes occurring in communities across the country.

The international evidence on what follows a ban is instructive. South Korea, which legislated against dog meat slaughter in 2024, cited public health improvement as a primary driver alongside shifting public attitudes. The Philippines enacted its ban in 1998 and recorded measurable reductions in rabies-linked incidents in affected provinces over the following decade. In both cases, enforcement became possible precisely because a clear legal line existed. You cannot enforce a standard that has never been set.

The conversation in Vietnam is already happening — and it is being led by Vietnamese people. A 2021 survey found that 95% of respondents in Vietnam support ending the dog and cat meat trade. Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have both issued formal guidance encouraging residents to stop consuming dog meat, citing public health and reputational concerns. The public will exists. The regulatory framework to match it does not — yet. What Vietnam's food safety authorities have the power to do is create the legal architecture that reflects what the population already believes.

Regulation is not the enemy of culture or livelihoods. It is the mechanism by which a society protects its people. A trade that cannot meet any standard of food safety inspection is, by definition, a trade that cannot be made safe. The path forward is the one that 95% of the Vietnamese public already supports: ending the dog meat trade, and replacing an unregulated vacuum with enforceable law. Lucky, a nine-year-old Ta dog and family companion, represents the millions of animals and the thousands of families that stand to benefit from exactly that change.

title: The Hidden Rabies Risk in Vietnam's Unregulated Dog Meat Trade
excerpt: Informal slaughter practices create direct exposure pathways for rabies and other zoonotic diseases. Without regulated facilities, the risk to workers and consumers remains unquantified and unmanaged.
body_html:
Vietnam's dog meat trade operates entirely outside the formal food safety system. There are zero registered slaughterhouses — meaning no inspections, no safety protocols, and no disease screening at any point in the supply chain.

Rabies is the most acute risk. Dogs transported long distances under extreme stress show suppressed immune responses, and informal slaughter conditions — often involving blunt force — create direct blood and saliva exposure for workers and bystanders. The Ho Chi Minh City Food Safety Management Authority has issued multiple consumption warnings in recent years, citing these exact pathways.

E. coli and Salmonella contamination are also endemic in unregulated meat handling environments. Without refrigeration, sanitation, or inspection, contamination rates in informal dog meat markets are significantly higher than in regulated meat sectors.

This is not a marginal issue. With an estimated 5 million dogs entering the trade annually, the scale of unregulated meat handling represents a genuine and ongoing public health risk — one that receives far less attention than it deserves.

95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending this trade — and the public health argument is one of the strongest reasons why. Sign the petition to demand regulated food safety standards and a permanent ban.

title: Stolen in the Night: How Pet Theft Feeds the Dog Meat Supply Chain
excerpt: Organised theft networks target family pets in both rural and urban Vietnam, transporting them hundreds of kilometres to informal markets. Many victims are beloved companions stolen from their homes.
body_html:
The dog meat supply chain in Vietnam runs significantly on stolen pets. Organised theft networks — some operating across multiple provinces — target family dogs in both rural villages and urban neighbourhoods, using poison bait, traps, and motorbike-mounted wire snares to capture animals quickly and quietly.

Dogs are crammed into wire mesh cages, often 10–20 animals per cage, without food, water, or veterinary care. They are then transported hundreds of kilometres to informal markets or directly to unlicensed slaughter points. By the time they arrive, many are severely dehydrated or injured.

For the families they were taken from, the loss is devastating. Dogs in Vietnam are not livestock — they are companions, protectors, and family members. The cultural and emotional bond between Vietnamese families and their dogs is precisely what makes this trade so deeply opposed by the public.

A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending the trade — a number that reflects widespread moral rejection, not fringe advocacy. The theft of family pets is cited as one of the top reasons for this overwhelming public consensus.

No registered slaughterhouse exists anywhere in Vietnam. This trade operates entirely in the shadows — and it thrives there. Sign the petition to demand accountability and a permanent ban.

title: 95% of Vietnamese Want the Trade to End. So Why Hasn't It?
excerpt: A 2021 survey found overwhelming public support for ending the dog meat trade in Vietnam. The barriers are political and economic — not cultural. Here's what's standing in the way.
body_html:
The data is unambiguous: 95% of Vietnamese respondents in a 2021 survey support ending the dog meat trade, explicitly rejecting the idea that it is a cultural necessity. This is not a fringe position — it is a supermajority mandate.

So why does the trade persist? The barriers are structural, not cultural. A small number of economic actors — traders, transport operators, and informal slaughter operators — have an active financial interest in maintaining the status quo. Without formal regulation, there is no mechanism to enforce a ban even if one were enacted tomorrow.

Political momentum has been slow. Local governments in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have issued advisory recommendations to reduce dog meat consumption, citing public health risks and international scrutiny. But advisory recommendations are not law, and enforcement is non-existent.

The path to change runs through the Communist Party of Vietnam and food safety authorities — the bodies with actual regulatory power. A sustained, locally-led campaign applying public pressure through formal petition channels is the most effective lever available.

This campaign exists to be that lever. Sign the petition and join the 95% who are already on the right side of this issue.

In every formal food sector in Vietnam, there is a regulatory baseline: registered facilities, inspection regimes, sanitation standards. The dog meat trade has none of these. There is not a single registered dog meat slaughterhouse in Vietnam — a fact confirmed by food safety authorities in Ho Chi Minh City.

This creates a food safety gap with no equivalent in the formal meat sector. Animals enter the supply chain with no health screening. Slaughter occurs in uncontrolled environments. Meat is handled and distributed without cold chain management or pathogen testing. Consumers have no way to assess the safety of what they are consuming.

The comparison to countries that have enacted bans is instructive. The Philippines banned the dog meat trade in 1998 under the Animal Welfare Act, and South Korea has been progressively restricting it through legislation. In both cases, the regulatory argument — food safety, public health, disease control — was as central as animal welfare in driving legislative change.

Vietnam has the public mandate to act. 95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending this trade. What is missing is political will and formal enforcement mechanisms. A petition directed at the Communist Party and food safety authorities is the most direct way to close that gap.

title: Lucky: The Dog Who Became the Face of a Movement
excerpt: For nine years, Lucky has been a priceless member of his Vietnamese family. His story — and why his owners decided they could no longer stay silent about the trade threatening dogs like him.
body_html:
Lucky is a purebred Vietnamese Ta dog — nine years old, with the quiet dignity of an animal who has spent his whole life as a treasured family companion. To his owners, he is not a pet in the casual sense. He is a presence in the home, a protector, a source of daily joy. He has a name. He has a history. He is, as his family says, a priceless treasure.

Lucky's story is the reason this campaign exists. Not because his situation is unique — but because it isn't. Across Vietnam, millions of dogs just like Lucky live in exactly this kind of bond with their families. And millions of them are at risk from a trade their owners never consented to.

Pet theft is rampant. Organised networks target dogs in both rural and urban areas. A dog like Lucky — healthy, well-fed, clearly cared for — is exactly the kind of target these networks seek out. The moment he leaves the garden, the risk becomes real.

Lucky's owners decided they could not stay silent. They knew that 95% of Vietnamese people share their values — that dogs are family members, not food — and that this shared belief is the foundation on which lasting change can be built.

This campaign is their voice, and the voice of every Vietnamese family that has lost a pet, or lives in fear of losing one. Sign the petition and stand with them.
